structure.title: A visitor's promise
structure.text: Beowulf travels to aid another king, entering a hall where hospitality and fear have become inseparable.

structure.title: Deeds across a lifetime
structure.text: The poem shifts from youthful achievement to later responsibilities, placing individual courage within the uncertain future of a people.

people.name: Beowulf
people.text: A young warrior from across the sea with the strength of thirty men, who comes to the Danish king to prove himself against a monster.

people.name: Hrothgar
people.text: The ageing king of the Danes, whose great mead-hall has been raided by night for twelve years and who can no longer defend it himself.

people.name: Grendel
people.text: A monster from the marshes, descended from Cain, who cannot bear the sound of feasting and comes in the dark to kill.

context.title: Gift and obligation
context.text: A lord's gifts and a warrior's loyalty bind a community. Public promises establish responsibilities and reputation.

context.title: Two horizons of belief
context.text: A Christian narrator recounts an earlier heroic world. The poem can honour its people while placing their beliefs at a distance.
context.takeaway: Narrator and characters occupy different perspectives.

notice.text: Listen to stories told within the hall.
notice.why: Earlier conflicts complicate the celebration of present success.
Material splendour can embody both community and vulnerability.

opening: A king builds a hall where his people can feast, hear songs, and feel secure together. Every night a creature comes to tear that security apart. Beowulf arrives from across the sea offering to fight it without a sword, staking his name on a promise nobody else can fulfil. The poem has the direct excitement of a monster story, surrounded by a darker knowledge: halls burn, loyalties fail, and a people cannot build a lasting future solely on the strength of one extraordinary man.
